stem: Groundwork: is the second sentence one example from a group, or the same claim stated more precisely? Choose the word or phrase that fits the blank.
stimulus: When the immune system meets the same pathogen a second time, its memory B cells respond in one notably different way. ______ they release antibodies that grip the pathogen far more tightly than the antibodies made during the first encounter.
explanation: The first sentence mentions one vague thing: 'one notably different way.' The second sentence says exactly what that one way is. There is no larger group to pick from, so you are zooming in on the same claim, and that calls for 'Specifically.' This sorting step comes before every SAT transition question that offers 'for example' and 'specifically' side by side.

A.why: You saw a general sentence followed by a detail and reached for 'for example.' But the first sentence names only one way, so the second sentence can't be one example out of several. It spells out that single way.

C.why: 'Even so' signals that the second sentence goes against the first. Here the second sentence agrees with the first and explains it. You may have read 'far more tightly' as a surprise. A surprising detail is not a contradiction.

D.why: 'Instead' means one thing replaces another. Nothing is being replaced here. The second sentence describes the different response the first sentence promised.

subtype_name: General claim, then the detail (For example vs Specifically / In particular)

stem: Groundwork: is the second sentence one example from a group, or the same claim stated more precisely? Choose the word or phrase that fits the blank.
stimulus: Sprint coaches rely on several drills to sharpen an athlete's start out of the blocks. ______ some have runners push a weighted sled for the first ten meters, building the force needed to drive forward from a crouch.
explanation: The first sentence names a group with a plural: 'several drills.' The second sentence picks out one member of that group, the weighted-sled drill. When one item is drawn from a larger set, use 'For example.' Learning to spot an umbrella noun followed by one of its members prepares you for SAT transition questions.

A.why: 'In other words' would mean the second sentence restates the whole first sentence. It doesn't. It adds new, narrower information about just one of the several drills.

B.why: 'However' needs a contradiction. The sled drill is one of the drills the first sentence mentions, so the two sentences point the same way.

D.why: 'Therefore' marks a result. Using several drills doesn't cause one drill to exist. The second sentence is an instance of the first, not a consequence of it.

stem: Groundwork: is the second sentence one example from a group, or the same claim stated more precisely? Choose the word or phrase that fits the blank.
stimulus: Over the centuries, English has absorbed many words from the languages of people its speakers met through travel and trade. ______ the word "kayak" came into English from Inuktitut, where it names a small, covered boat built for hunting at sea.
explanation: 'Many words' is a plural group. The second sentence gives one word from that group, 'kayak.' A single sample taken from a larger set is an example, so 'For example' fits. This is the same check you'll make on SAT transition questions that open with a broad claim about 'many' or 'several' things.

A.why: 'In other words' says the second sentence repeats the first in different wording. It doesn't. It brings in a new detail about one particular word instead of restating the general claim about many words.

B.why: 'In contrast' needs two things that differ. 'Kayak' is one of the borrowed words, so it supports the first sentence.

C.why: 'Finally' marks the last step in a sequence or list. The passage gives no list of steps, and nothing suggests 'kayak' was the last word borrowed.

stem: Groundwork: is the second sentence one example from a group, or the same claim stated more precisely? Choose the word or phrase that fits the blank.
stimulus: Researchers who examined fossil leaves from an ancient lakebed in Wyoming noticed that the leaves shared one unusual trait. ______ every leaf had small teeth along only the upper half of its edge, a pattern seldom seen in living plants.
explanation: The first sentence mentions a single, unnamed thing: 'one unusual trait.' The second sentence says exactly what that trait was. Because you are zooming in on the same claim and not choosing from a set, 'Specifically' is correct. Telling an exact spelling-out apart from a sample is the core move in SAT transition questions that pair 'for example' with 'specifically.'

B.why: You treated the detail as a sample from a group. But the first sentence names only one trait, and the second sentence describes it. There are no other traits for it to be an example of.

C.why: 'On the other hand' brings in an opposing point. The second sentence agrees with the first by naming the trait it promised, so nothing is being opposed.

D.why: 'Similarly' adds a second, parallel point. The second sentence doesn't describe a new thing that resembles the first. It explains the same trait in detail.
